objectives: Master bilateral diplomacy + embassy architecture — sections, accreditation, agrément, recall, diplomatic ranks.
Master the Fisher-Ury-Patton *Getting to Yes* framework + BATNA + ZOPA + interest-based negotiation.
Master Putnam's two-level game theory + Lax + Sebenius 3D Negotiation + bargaining theory.

slides.title: Embassies + bilateral architecture: from credentials to chanceries
slides.body:
**Bilateral diplomacy** = the conduct of relations between two sovereign states through accredited representatives, embassies, + direct negotiation. It remains the *core unit* of diplomatic practice — even multilateral institutions ultimately rest on bilateral relationships among their members.

**The embassy as institution**. A modern embassy is a complex organization — typically the largest single foreign installation a state operates abroad. Key components:
- **Head of mission** — *ambassador* (the highest rank, accredited head-of-state-to-head-of-state) or *chargé d'affaires* (interim head between ambassadors). Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961 Article 14 establishes the three classes (ambassadors + papal nuncios; envoys + ministers plenipotentiary; chargés d'affaires).
- **Deputy chief of mission (DCM)** — the embassy's chief operating officer + second-in-command.
- **Political section** — reports on host-country politics + represents the sending state's views to the host government.
- **Economic section** — reports on host economy + commercial environment; supports trade promotion.
- **Consular section** — visas + citizen services + protection of nationals (cross-ref consular-affairs-and-protocol).
- **Defense attaché office** — uniformed military liaison + reporting.
- **Public affairs / cultural section** — press, media, public diplomacy, cultural exchanges.
- **Management section** — administration, security, real property, IT.
- **Intelligence section** — declared + undeclared liaison + collection (governed by separate national authorities; embassy provides cover + diplomatic protection but operationally is distinct).
- **Specialized attachés** — agriculture, science, law enforcement, immigration, treasury, energy, depending on the bilateral relationship's intensity.

**Accreditation + the agrément process**:
- **Step 1 — selection** by the sending state (typically the foreign minister + head of state).
- **Step 2 — request for *agrément*** — the sending state confidentially asks the receiving state whether the proposed ambassador is acceptable. *Agrément* may be granted or quietly refused; refusal is rare + diplomatically delicate; the practice avoids public embarrassment.
- **Step 3 — appointment + commission**.
- **Step 4 — presentation of credentials** — the ambassador presents *letters of credence* (signed by the sending head of state + addressed to the receiving head of state) at a formal ceremony. The ambassador's tenure officially begins at the moment of presentation.
- **Step 5 — recall + farewell** — the ambassador presents *letters of recall* at departure.
- **Persona non grata (PNG)** — Vienna Convention Art. 9 — the receiving state may at any time declare any member of mission *non grata* + require their removal, *without giving reasons*. This is the primary non-violent sanction in bilateral relations + a frequent diplomatic signal (e.g., Western expulsions of Russian diplomats after Skripal poisoning 2018; mass post-Ukraine expulsions 2022-23).

**Diplomatic ranks (Vienna Convention 1961 codification)**:
- **Ambassador extraordinary + plenipotentiary** — full powers; accredited head-of-state-to-head-of-state.
- **Envoy extraordinary + minister plenipotentiary** — historical rank; rarely used today.
- **Minister resident** — historical; rarely used.
- **Chargé d'affaires** *en pied* (permanent, accredited foreign-minister-to-foreign-minister) — used when full ambassadorial relations are not established.
- **Chargé d'affaires *ad interim*** — the DCM or senior officer running the embassy between ambassadors or during the ambassador's absence.
- *Precedence* among ambassadors is determined by the date of presentation of credentials; the longest-serving is the **doyen** (or *dean*) of the diplomatic corps + speaks ceremonially on behalf of the corps.

**Bilateral relationship management** — the embassy is the *steady-state* infrastructure; ministerial visits + summit diplomacy + special envoys are the *high-tempo* layer. *Strategic dialogues* + *2+2 meetings* (foreign + defense ministers) + *commissions* + *working groups* structure ongoing engagement. *Joint statements* + *communiqués* + *memoranda of understanding (MOUs)* + *executive agreements* + *treaties* are the documentary outputs (cross-ref international-law-treaties on the legal hierarchy).

**Alliance + partnership tiers** — bilateral relationships are typically formalized in tiers:
- **Treaty allies** — mutual defense commitments under formal treaties (U.S. has ~5 bilateral treaty allies — Japan 1960, ROK 1953, Philippines 1951, Australia + NZ via ANZUS 1951, Thailand via Manila Pact 1954 — + 30 NATO allies via Washington Treaty Art. 5).
- **Major non-NATO ally (MNNA)** — U.S. statutory category (Foreign Assistance Act 1961, expanded 1989) granting privileged defense + economic + intelligence cooperation without mutual defense (currently ~20 countries including Israel, Egypt, Japan, ROK, Australia, NZ, Argentina, Brazil, Pakistan, Philippines, Thailand, Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Morocco, Tunisia, Afghanistan (pre-2021), Qatar, Colombia, Taiwan (de facto), Kenya).
- **Strategic partnership** — varying scopes (U.S.-India *2+2*; EU strategic partnerships; China's *all-weather strategic partnerships*).
- **Comprehensive economic partnership** — RCEP, CPTPP, USMCA, EU-Japan EPA.
- **Normal diplomatic relations** — full embassies + consular relations.
- **Reduced relations** — chargé d'affaires level; severed relations; no relations.

[viz:alliance-network — focus on NATO + the U.S. treaty-ally hub-and-spoke + the post-2022 expansions to Finland (2023) + Sweden (2024) + the global Indo-Pacific 'plus' partnerships — Japan, ROK, Australia, NZ, the Quad, AUKUS.]

slides.title: Fisher-Ury-Patton + BATNA + ZOPA: the principled-negotiation revolution
slides.body:
**The Harvard Negotiation Project** (founded 1979 at Harvard Law School) revolutionized the *theory* + *practice* of negotiation. The flagship work — Roger **Fisher**, William **Ury**, + (in later editions) Bruce **Patton** — ***Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In*** (1981; 2nd ed. 1991; 3rd ed. 2011). >15 million copies; translated into >35 languages; the most influential negotiation text of the 20th century + foundational for U.S. + many other states' diplomatic training.

**The four principles of *principled negotiation***:
1. **Separate the people from the problem** — attack the issue + not the person; build personal rapport + emotional space; manage perception + emotion + communication explicitly. *Position* vs *relationship* — both matter.
2. **Focus on interests, not positions** — *positions* are stated demands; *interests* are the underlying needs + concerns + fears + aspirations that motivate them. Multiple positions can satisfy a single interest; multiple interests can underlie a single position. The Fisher-Ury *orange* parable — two sisters fight over an orange; an interest-based question reveals one wants the juice + the other the peel. *Interest-based bargaining* opens creative tradeoffs that positional bargaining forecloses.
3. **Invent options for mutual gain** — separate inventing from deciding; brainstorm broad sets of possible agreements; look for *integrative* solutions (expanding the pie) before *distributive* ones (dividing it). Mary Parker Follett's 1920s integrative-bargaining work prefigured this; Lax + Sebenius's *value creation* extends it (next slide).
4. **Insist on using objective criteria** — appeal to fair standards (precedent, market value, scientific judgment, professional norms, legal precedent) rather than will-against-will. Reduces face-saving costs of moving toward agreement.

**BATNA — Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement** (Fisher + Ury). Possibly the single most-cited concept in negotiation theory.
- **BATNA** = what you will do if the negotiation fails. Your BATNA is the *floor* below which you should not accept any agreement.
- **Strong BATNA** → confidence + willingness to walk away → bargaining leverage.
- **Weak BATNA** → desperation → vulnerable to exploitation.
- The negotiator's first preparatory task: assess *your own* BATNA + your *counterpart's* BATNA. *Improving your BATNA* (e.g., cultivating alternative partners + readiness for the next round) is often the highest-leverage move *outside* the negotiation room.
- **Reservation value** (or *reservation price*) — the worst outcome you would still accept; derived from the BATNA. In international negotiations, the reservation value often includes political + reputational costs as well as substantive ones.

**ZOPA — Zone of Possible Agreement**:
- **ZOPA** = the overlap between the parties' reservation values. If A's reservation is *worst case A accepts* + B's reservation is *worst case B accepts*, ZOPA exists when there is any deal both prefer to their respective BATNAs.
- **Positive ZOPA** → agreement is possible.
- **Negative ZOPA** → no agreement possible; either negotiate to *change* preferences or change BATNAs, or accept impasse.
- The negotiator's task: identify whether ZOPA exists, what its boundaries are, + where within ZOPA the deal will likely settle (informed by relative bargaining power, urgency, alternatives, + skill).

**Anchoring, framing, + cognitive biases** — drawing on Kahneman + Tversky.
- **Anchoring** — the first number named exerts disproportionate gravitational pull on the eventual outcome. *First-mover anchor* is often advantageous when you have strong information; *reactive devaluation* + *re-anchoring* counter it.
- **Framing effects** — gain vs loss framing shapes risk-taking + concession behavior; the same outcome described as a *concession from current position* vs *gain from worst case* induces different responses.
- **Reactive devaluation** — proposals presented by an adversary are systematically devalued by the recipient; mediator + Track II channels can mitigate.
- **Overconfidence + the *fixed-pie* bias** — negotiators systematically overestimate their own positions + underestimate joint-gain potential. Training + role-play + structured preparation mitigate.

**William Ury's *Getting Past No*** (1993) + ***The Power of a Positive No*** (2007) + ***Getting to Yes with Yourself*** (2015). Ury developed the framework into a *breakthrough negotiation* method for difficult counterparts. *Going to the balcony* — pause + perspective; *step to their side*; *reframe*; *build them a golden bridge*; *make it hard to say no*. Widely used in diplomatic + commercial + interpersonal contexts.

**Howard Raiffa — *The Art and Science of Negotiation*** (1982) + ***Negotiation Analysis*** (2002). Decision-theoretic + game-theoretic foundations of negotiation. Raiffa systematized *negotiation analysis* as a decision-science subfield — analyzing the negotiation problem from the analyst's chair + then deploying tactics.

**Deepak Malhotra + Max Bazerman — *Negotiation Genius*** (2007); Bazerman *Judgment in Managerial Decision Making* (1986+). The behavioral-decision tradition's negotiation textbook + foundational work on cognitive biases in negotiation.

**Application to bilateral diplomacy** — the Fisher-Ury framework underlies modern diplomatic training. The U.S. Foreign Service Institute, the Diplomatic Academy of Vienna, Sciences Po, the Fletcher School, + the Geneva Centre for Security Policy all teach *Getting to Yes* as foundational reading. *Interest-based bargaining* + *BATNA* + *ZOPA* are now diplomatic vernacular. Cross-ref Camp David (Carter + Brzezinski + Begin + Sadat 1978) + Oslo (Norwegian backchannel 1993) + Dayton (Holbrooke 1995) + Good Friday (Mitchell 1998) + JCPOA (Kerry + Zarif + the P5+1 2015) — each a case study in interest-based negotiation under hard constraints.

slides.title: Putnam two-level games + Lax + Sebenius 3D + the modern bargaining frontier
slides.body:
**Robert Putnam — *Diplomacy and Domestic Politics: The Logic of Two-Level Games*** (1988 *International Organization*). Harvard. The foundational theoretical framework for understanding international negotiations as the simultaneous interplay of two interlocked games:
- **Level I** — *international bargaining* between national negotiators.
- **Level II** — *domestic ratification + political acceptability* within each country.

Putnam's central insight: any international agreement requires *win-sets* — the set of Level I agreements that would be ratified by the relevant domestic constituency.
- **Larger win-set** → greater likelihood of agreement (more overlap with the other side's win-set).
- **Smaller win-set** → greater bargaining leverage (you can credibly say *my hands are tied; my parliament will not accept*) but greater risk of involuntary defection (the agreement fails to ratify).
- The negotiator who *wants* a deal will try to *expand* the other side's win-set + sometimes their own; the negotiator who *wants leverage* will *visibly constrain* their own win-set (the *Schelling commitment*; cross-ref crisis-and-conflict-resolution).
- **Synergistic linkages** — Level I tradeoffs that improve Level II political feasibility on both sides.
- **Involuntary defection** — the negotiator agrees in good faith but cannot deliver ratification (Wilson + the U.S. Senate's 1919 rejection of Versailles + League of Nations membership is the canonical case; Clinton + the 1997 Kyoto Protocol failure to ratify; Obama + the post-2017 JCPOA exit by Trump is a related dynamic).

**Putnam's framework explains**:
- Why governments are sometimes *better off* with tighter domestic constraints — Senate skepticism strengthens U.S. negotiators' hand at the bargaining table (*Schelling commitment*).
- Why diplomats spend so much time on *domestic political signaling* during negotiations — they are managing Level II while also negotiating Level I.
- Why *executive-led* fast-track / TPA / trade-promotion-authority arrangements matter — they constrain Level II to expedite Level I.
- Why backchannel + informal channels matter — they allow exploration of Level I deals without committing Level II constituencies.
- Cross-ref Helen V. Milner *Interests, Institutions, and Information* (1997) — extended Putnam to domestic political institutions + information.

**David Lax + James Sebenius — *3-D Negotiation: Powerful Tools to Change the Game in Your Most Important Deals*** (2006). Harvard Business School + Harvard Law School. Built on *The Manager as Negotiator* (1986). The 3-D framework:
- **1D — Tactics** at the table — the standard *Getting to Yes* + Bazerman + Malhotra material.
- **2D — Deal design** — substantive architecture of the deal — what packages of issues + contingencies + sequencing maximize joint value + meet both parties' interests.
- **3D — Setup** — *who, what, when, where, how* before the table — *negotiation setup* + *party selection* + *agenda* + *sequencing* + *backchannels* + *timing* + *coalition design* + *no-deal options*. The 3D claim: most negotiation value is created or destroyed *before* the parties sit down — by setup choices that determine who is at the table + what is on it.

**Sebenius's diplomatic + commercial work** — extensive consulting on U.S. + international negotiations + executive education at Harvard Kennedy + Business Schools.

**Coalitional + multiparty bargaining** — beyond Putnam's two-level dyad.
- **William Riker *The Theory of Political Coalitions*** (1962) — minimum winning coalitions.
- **Nash bargaining solution** (Nash 1950) — under certain axioms, the unique fair bargaining outcome maximizes the product of utilities above the disagreement point.
- **Rubinstein bargaining model** (Rubinstein 1982) — alternating-offers infinite-horizon bargaining; the negotiator with lower time preference (more patience) gets a larger share.
- **Coalitional game theory + the *core* + the *Shapley value*** — for multilateral negotiations (cross-ref multilateral-institutions-and-un).

**Modern bargaining + IR theory**:
- **James Fearon — *Rationalist Explanations for War*** (1995 *International Organization*) — bargaining-theory account of war as bargaining failure under (a) commitment problems + (b) private information / incentives to misrepresent + (c) issue indivisibility. The dominant rationalist IR account of war + bargaining.
- **Robert Powell — *In the Shadow of Power*** (1999) + bargaining + commitment problems.
- **Robert Jervis — *Perception and Misperception in International Politics*** (1976) + the security dilemma + intelligence + signaling.
- **Thomas Schelling — *The Strategy of Conflict*** (1960) + *Arms and Influence* (1966) — *focal points* + *commitment* + *credible threats* + *coercion* + *bargaining with binoculars*. Nobel 2005. Cross-ref crisis-and-conflict-resolution.

**Cultural + cross-cultural negotiation**:
- **Edward Hall — *Beyond Culture*** (1976) — high-context vs low-context communication.
- **Geert Hofstede — *Culture's Consequences*** (1980) — cultural dimensions (power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, etc.).
- **Erin Meyer — *The Culture Map*** (2014) — practical cross-cultural negotiation framework.
- **Jeswald Salacuse — *The Global Negotiator*** (2003) — cross-cultural diplomatic + commercial negotiation.
- **Raymond Cohen — *Negotiating Across Cultures*** (1991 + 1997) — diplomatic-specific cross-cultural analysis.

**Mearsheimer + structural realism on bargaining**. John **Mearsheimer** *The Tragedy of Great Power Politics* (2001) + offensive realism — great-power negotiations are constrained by *structural anarchy* + relative-gains concerns; cooperation is fragile + always conditioned on the shadow of the future + relative-power calculations. Mearsheimer's framework is the realist counterpoint to liberal-institutionalist accounts of bargaining + cooperation.

**Practical bilateral negotiation workflow** — what a foreign-service officer actually does.
- **Preparation**: define interests + positions + BATNA + ZOPA + counterparts' likely positions + Level II constraints both sides + drafting + briefing + clearance.
- **Approach**: opening, agenda, sequencing, atmosphere, rapport.
- **Substantive negotiation**: information exchange + proposal + counter-proposal + concession patterns + multi-issue tradeoffs + packaging + integrative move-making.
- **Pre-closing**: text refinement, asterisks, language ambiguity (constructive or destructive), parking issues, scope adjustments.
- **Closure**: initialing, signing, joint statement, communiqué, side letters, MOUs.
- **Post-agreement**: ratification, implementation, monitoring, dispute resolution, renegotiation.

**Lessons from canonical cases**: Camp David 1978 (Carter mediation; Sadat-Begin trust-building); Oslo 1993 (Norwegian backchannel; track II to track I escalation); Dayton 1995 (Holbrooke + intensive isolation + power-balancing among Serb-Croat-Muslim factions); JCPOA 2015 (Kerry + Zarif + Sherman + Mogherini + the technical-political interplay over 18 months + the Level II Senate constraint); Brexit negotiations (Barnier + Frost + the EU-UK Level II + Level I interplay 2017-2020); U.S.-China Phase One trade deal 2020 (Lighthizer + Liu He + the Trump-Xi summit-level theatrics).

question.question: Walk through a BATNA + ZOPA analysis for a bilateral fisheries agreement
question.goal: Two coastal states A + B share an overlapping EEZ + are negotiating annual fishing quotas. Compute BATNAs + identify ZOPA + recommend a strategy.

steps.prompt: What is each side's BATNA if no agreement is reached?

acceptedAnswers: the status quo of contested fishing with enforcement incidents stock decline and the risk of escalation to a wider dispute possibly going to itlos or the icj

steps.reveal: **Each side's BATNA** under no-deal = unilateral assertion of fishing rights in contested zone; enforcement encounters between fisheries patrol vessels; risk of escalation to diplomatic incident; ongoing fish-stock degradation from uncoordinated harvesting (the classic *tragedy of the commons*); + possible legal proceedings before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) or arbitration under UNCLOS Part XV. *Both BATNAs are bad* — costly enforcement, stock collapse, legal risk, political fallout. Bad mutual BATNAs are *favorable* for negotiation: there is strong joint interest in any deal that improves on the no-deal trajectory.

acceptedAnswers: estimate each side's reservation value as the worst quota that beats its batna then check whether the two reservation values overlap such that a quota allocation exists that both prefer to the no deal trajectory

steps.reveal: **ZOPA analysis**: estimate each side's *reservation value* — the worst quota allocation it would still accept rather than walk away. A's reservation might be ~30% of historical catch (below which fleet livelihoods collapse + political costs exceed BATNA costs). B's reservation might similarly be ~40% (B has higher fleet capacity + greater political dependence on the fishery). If A would accept a quota giving it ≥30% of the joint quota + B would accept a quota giving it ≥40% (i.e., A taking ≤60%), then ZOPA = quotas where A takes 30-60% (so B takes 40-70%). Positive ZOPA → agreement zone exists. The deal will settle within ZOPA depending on bargaining skill, anchoring, urgency, third-party leverage.

steps.prompt: Apply Fisher-Ury — what interest-based moves expand the pie?

acceptedAnswers: look for tradeable interests beyond raw quota numbers like seasonality stock conservation enforcement cooperation processing rights port access scientific collaboration joint vessel monitoring and link to wider economic or maritime issues that expand joint gains

steps.reveal: **Interest-based moves expanding the pie**: (1) *Multi-issue packaging* — quota + seasonality + species mix + processing rights + port access + scientific cooperation + enforcement-sharing; trade across issues where the two sides have different intensities. (2) *Conservation linkage* — if both fleets reduce harvest temporarily, stock recovers + total long-run catch increases for both — pareto-improving over the over-fishing equilibrium. (3) *Wider linkage* — couple the fisheries deal to a maritime-cooperation framework (joint search-and-rescue, hydrographic survey, marine science) producing political + reputational gains. (4) *Third-party guarantees* — World Bank or regional fisheries body monitoring builds credibility. (5) *Sunsetting + renegotiation clauses* — reduce risk of long-term lock-in + Level II resistance.

steps.prompt: How does Putnam's two-level framework refine the strategy?

acceptedAnswers: each negotiator must assess the win sets at home including fishing industry coastal communities environmental ngos and parliament a tight domestic constraint can be used as bargaining leverage but risks involuntary defection so the negotiators may engage in synergistic linkage strategies and coordinate domestic communication

steps.reveal: **Putnam refinement**: each negotiator faces a Level II constituency — fishing industry, coastal communities, environmental NGOs, opposition parties, parliament. The *win-set* is the set of Level I deals each can ratify domestically. (1) *Tight win-set* can be *used* as bargaining leverage (*my parliament will not accept less than X*) — Schelling commitment. (2) But tight win-set risks *involuntary defection* — the deal fails to ratify. (3) *Synergistic linkages* — deal elements that satisfy both Level IIs simultaneously (e.g., joint scientific projects that fund both countries' marine biologists; conservation language that satisfies environmental NGOs in both). (4) *Domestic communication* — pre-brief key Level II actors; manage media; identify champions. (5) *Pre-clear* with key constituencies before signature. Strategy combines Fisher-Ury at Level I with active Level II management.

question.question: Why is BATNA the most-cited concept in modern negotiation theory?
options: BATNA — Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — was coined by Roger Fisher + William Ury in *Getting to Yes* (1981). It is the answer to the question: *what will you do if the negotiation fails?* Three reasons it became foundational: (1) **It defines your floor** — you should never accept a deal worse than your BATNA, so identifying it explicitly prevents value-destroying concessions under pressure. (2) **It generates leverage** — a strong BATNA (alternative partners, ability to walk away) enables credible firmness; a weak BATNA makes you vulnerable to exploitation. (3) **It points to highest-leverage strategy outside the room** — *improving your BATNA* (cultivating alternatives, building patience, securing fallback resources) is often more valuable than tactical moves inside the room. BATNA is paired with ZOPA (Zone of Possible Agreement = overlap of parties' reservation values). Together they convert negotiation from intuition to analysis. Used throughout diplomacy (Camp David, Oslo, Dayton, JCPOA, Brexit) + commercial + interpersonal contexts. Lax + Sebenius's *3D Negotiation* + Putnam's two-level games extend the framework.
question.explanation: BATNA (Fisher + Ury *Getting to Yes* 1981) = what you do if negotiation fails. (1) Defines floor — never accept worse than BATNA. (2) Generates leverage — strong BATNA enables credible firmness. (3) Points to highest-leverage moves outside the room — improving BATNA. Paired with ZOPA (overlap of reservation values). Foundational for diplomatic + commercial + interpersonal negotiation; extended by Lax + Sebenius 3D + Putnam two-level games.

How is it paired with ZOPA?

Defines floor (never accept worse), generates leverage (strong BATNA = credible firmness), + points to high-leverage moves outside the room. Paired with ZOPA. question.question: Negotiate a bilateral semiconductor cooperation agreement
question.prompt: You are deputy assistant secretary for economic affairs preparing for bilateral talks with country X (a major chip-fabrication economy) on a U.S.-X semiconductor cooperation framework. The U.S. side wants: X's commitment to coordinate export controls on advanced chips to China, X's investment in U.S. fabs, + reciprocal market access. X wants: relief from extraterritorial U.S. export controls on legacy chips, technology-sharing on advanced packaging, + visa facilitation for engineers. Write a ≤220-word memo for the assistant secretary applying (a) Fisher-Ury interests-not-positions analysis + BATNA + ZOPA estimation; (b) Putnam two-level game with explicit identification of Level II constraints on both sides (Congress, the chip industry, allies, opposition parties in X); + (c) Lax + Sebenius 3D — *setup* recommendations including which other parties (Japan, ROK, Netherlands) should be brought into the conversation + sequencing of the talks.

question.question: Country A's reservation value on annual quota share is $r_A = 0.30$ (30%); country B's reservation value on its share is $r_B = 0.40$ (40%). Compute the *width* of the zone of possible agreement $W = (1 - r_A) - r_B = 1 - r_A - r_B$ as a fraction of the joint quota.
question.hint: $W = 1 - r_A - r_B = 1 - 0.30 - 0.40 = 0.30 = 30\%$. A accepts ≥ 30% so A takes 30-60%; B accepts ≥ 40% so B takes 40-70%. Width = 30% of joint quota. Positive ZOPA → agreement possible. Negative ZOPA (if $r_A + r_B > 1$) would mean impasse + would require BATNA improvement, interest reframing, or third-party leverage to open.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain bilateral diplomatic negotiation by integrating (a) embassy + accreditation architecture (Vienna Convention 1961, *agrément*, PNG, diplomatic ranks); (b) Fisher-Ury-Patton *Getting to Yes* framework + BATNA + ZOPA; + (c) Putnam two-level games + Lax + Sebenius 3D Negotiation. Identify two canonical cases (Camp David, Oslo, Dayton, JCPOA, U.S.-China) that illustrate the integration.
question.rubric: Mentions: **Embassy architecture** — VCDR 1961 Art. 3 functions + Art. 4 *agrément* + Art. 9 *persona non grata* + Art. 14 ambassadorial ranks + Art. 22-24 inviolability; embassy sections (political, economic, consular, defense, public-affairs, intelligence); ambassador + DCM + presentation of credentials + doyen of the corps. **Fisher-Ury-Patton** *Getting to Yes* (1981) four principles — separate people from problem, focus on interests not positions, invent options for mutual gain, insist on objective criteria; **BATNA** (best alternative; defines floor + leverage) + **ZOPA** (zone of possible agreement = overlap of reservation values). Ury *Getting Past No* (1993). Raiffa *Negotiation Analysis*. Bazerman + Malhotra cognitive biases (anchoring, framing, reactive devaluation). **Putnam two-level games** (1988 *IO*) — Level I international + Level II domestic ratification; win-sets; synergistic linkage; involuntary defection (Wilson + 1919 Senate). **Lax + Sebenius 3D** — tactics + deal design + setup; most value created or destroyed in setup. Cases: Camp David 1978 (Carter + Sadat + Begin); Oslo 1993 (Norwegian backchannel); Dayton 1995 (Holbrooke); JCPOA 2015 (Kerry + Zarif + Sherman + the P5+1 + Senate constraint); U.S.-China trade Phase One 2020 (Lighthizer + Liu He). Concludes that bilateral diplomacy integrates institutional infrastructure + interest-based negotiation theory + two-level political-economy analysis + setup-stage strategic design.
